summary:
In the near future, humanity faces the task of expanding its understanding of
space, in particular studying planetary bodies in order to build permanent bases
on the Moon and to gather information about Mars during crewed or rover missions.
LithoTwin will help researchers prepare for these interplanetary tasks by analogy,
with the help of our home “blue marble”. We studied 19 sites on Earth and compared
them with the targets of exploration, the Moon and Mars. We used authoritative
published sources, compared the ground materials at the sites of interest and at
the targets, and added satellite images and relief models for clarity. To make it
comfortable for you, our team built the product as an interactive website.
We are a team of ambitious geologists from Kazan Federal University and
programmers from Moscow State University. The NASA hackathon gave us a unique
opportunity to pursue our ambition of studying and comparing the geology of
planetary bodies.
details:
What it does. LithoTwin answers one question: where on Earth should we rehearse a specific Moon or Mars mission? Pick a target and a task: a Moon base at the Shackleton crater rim, rover & EVA or drilling at Arcadia Planitia or Jezero crater on Mars. LithoTwin ranks 19 Earth sites (10 known analogs, 7 Russian candidates, 2 negative controls) on a 3D globe. Pentagon size shows similarity, colour shows suitability (bare ground, access, flat area for a base, slopes for a rover, a drill target), the number shows rank. Every site has a dossier: a three-line verdict, what makes up its score, its relief next to the target's, the suitability rules it passes or fails, satellite images and sources. A Russia mode shows where Russian sites stand in the world ranking. The app works in English and Russian.

How it works. For every site and target we resample the elevation model to a 500 m grid in a local equidistant projection and take five relief features over a 3 km circle: median slope, 90th-percentile slope, share of flat ground, detrended roughness and local relief. The team's geologists assign rock type (7 classes), ground ice (0-3), bare ground and access from the literature. Each feature becomes a similarity from 0 to 1; a task-specific weighted mean gives the score, and surface exposure adds up to 20 points. Suitability is a separate traffic light and is never mixed into the score.

Is it valid? For each of the 5 target-task pairs, the best negative control (Amazon rainforest, Kansas farmland) must score below the median of known analogs from the literature, and the result must hold when all weights are shifted by up to 20% (50 runs). All 5 pairs pass; 4 hold in 50 of 50 runs, one in 49 of 50. Satellite images also caught a data error during the hackathon: the Amazon control first sat in the city of Manaus and was moved into the forest.

Why it matters. Analog sites cost money and time to reach. LithoTwin makes the choice transparent and repeatable and adds new candidates: Chara Sands (Transbaikalia) ranks first in the world for rover tests at Arcadia, the Batagaika megaslump second for drilling ice-rich ground, and a Russian site is in the world top 3 for all five tasks.

Tools: JavaScript (Vite, globe.gl, three.js, d3-geo), Python (rasterio, numpy) for the data pipeline, GitHub Pages for hosting. Open source under the MIT license: https://github.com/wnfeelsgood-boop/LithoTwin
